One payment or monthly income: chart the cash calendar before comparing illness cover

Four interactive graphics compare two independently approved benefit schedules, their cash paths, required opening reserves and the effect of a delayed one-time receipt.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two independently confirmed payment calendars

Interactive planning lab

Additional starting cash · monthly scenario$5,000
Benefits received · one-time / monthly$50,000 / $54,000

Original hypothetical CAD cash calendars. A and B are independent alternatives with entered net receipts, not premiums or claim quotations. Do not add them: the model makes no finding that both claims qualify or can be paid together. Supply amounts and receipt dates confirmed after tax and any offsets. Every month adds receipts before paying recurring spending and the month-1 extra cost. Month 0 is opening cash. No within-month payment delay, interest, borrowing, inflation, policy eligibility, medical diagnosis, premium cost or recovery income is calculated. A negative cash point is an unfunded position. Receipts beyond the selected horizon are excluded, without a future settlement credit.

  1. Begin with the payment trigger, before the amount

The central idea

A lump sum and a stream of monthly receipts meet different cash calendars. Confirm the claim conditions first, then compare spendable amounts and dates with the costs they must fund.

01

Begin with the payment trigger, before the amount

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s health-insurance overview describes critical illness insurance as usually providing a one-time payment following a covered diagnosis. Definitions and covered conditions vary by insurer. A policy document and a claim decision determine whether a particular event qualifies.

FCAC’s disability-insurance overview describes protection when a person cannot work and earn income. Definitions, payment limits, duration and receipt delays require checking. A diagnosis and an inability to work are different questions; neither by itself establishes that both contracts will pay.

The calculator begins after those questions have been resolved for each alternative. Scenario A receives one independently entered net amount. Scenario B receives a net monthly amount for an independently entered number of months. It does not add the alternatives together. Any tax and offset adjustments must already be reflected in the supplied receipts.

02

Put the household costs on the same monthly calendar

The example runs for eighteen whole months. Recurring spending is CAD 4,500 a month, while other spendable income contributes CAD 1,500. A separate CAD 6,000 cost occurs in month one. The household begins with CAD 10,000 of accessible cash.

Scenario A receives CAD 50,000 in month two. Scenario B receives CAD 4,500 a month beginning in month four, with twelve payments ending in month fifteen. Their benefit totals are therefore CAD 50,000 and CAD 54,000 within the displayed window. These numbers are authored examples, not advertised benefits or estimates of an actual claim.

The event chart highlights months around the first payment, the one-time receipt and the monthly stream’s end. It shows benefit receipts only. The complete month-end cash paths then add other income and subtract both recurring and initial costs. Keeping those two views distinct helps explain why a large benefit bar need not mean a large remaining balance.

Every month receives its inflows before its costs are paid. That is a simplifying order. If rent leaves before a benefit arrives in the same month, the practical bank balance may need an additional buffer. Use actual dates for an implemented household plan.

03

Find the deepest shortfall rather than reading only the final balance

Before any benefit receipt, month one uses CAD 9,000 more than other income supplies. Under the one-time scenario, the month-two payment replenishes cash, but continuing spending draws it down again. The path ends month eighteen with CAD 0 at the selected CAD 10,000 opening balance.

The monthly scenario must first fund three months before its first benefit receipt. Those months create a cumulative CAD 15,000 deficit. During months four through fifteen, benefit payments and other income exceed recurring spending by CAD 1,500 a month. The final three months have no modeled benefit and consume CAD 3,000 each. The ending balance is CAD 4,000, but an earlier point still falls below zero.

Scenario A requires CAD 10,000 at the start to fund its entire calendar. Scenario B requires CAD 15,000, making its additional requirement CAD 5,000 above the selected cash. The higher ending balance in B does not make the early payments affordable on their due dates.

Required opening cash is the largest cumulative shortfall across the horizon, with a floor of zero. Additional opening cash subtracts the accessible reserve already entered. A negative plotted position remains an unfunded need; the tool creates no overdraft, borrowing facility or interest charge to fill it.

04

Test what changes when a payment arrives later

The matrix changes only scenario A’s net amount and receipt month. Spending, other income, the initial cost and accessible cash stay fixed. Each cell reports additional opening cash, rather than total benefits or a probability.

A larger payment can improve the final balance without funding the months before it arrives. Moving the same CAD 50,000 receipt from month two to month twelve leaves eleven earlier months to finance. Their cumulative deficit is CAD 39,000, so the extra opening requirement becomes CAD 29,000 above the selected CAD 10,000.

The columns are stress assumptions. They do not represent promised insurer processing times or contractual choices. If a selected receipt falls after the displayed horizon, it contributes nothing within that window. The tool does not credit a future payment against an earlier deficit or assume the household can borrow against it.

Likewise, the monthly stream’s maximum payment count is an entered calendar limit. It does not calculate an expiry age, a change in the definition of disability or an extension of coverage. Changing the horizon can expose months after the entered stream has ended.

05

Take the calendar back to the actual contracts and budget

Confirm the covered event, required evidence, applicable conditions, benefit amount and timing separately for each contract. FCAC identifies tax treatment and benefit offsets as points to check for disability cover. Do not enter a gross quoted amount as spendable cash unless the deductions have been assessed.

Next, replace the example’s costs with a household budget. Separate recurring commitments from one-time changes, identify income that would continue, and count only accessible resources assigned to this purpose. Property value or an inaccessible retirement balance cannot automatically pay this month’s bill.

Finally, compare premiums, exclusions and protection periods outside this cash exercise. A smaller reserve need under one assumed claim does not establish that a product offers broader cover or better value. These graphics explain payment shape and funding timing; they cannot select insurance or resolve a claim.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All dollar amounts and receipt dates are original hypothetical inputs. The tool compares independent scenarios A and B. It does not combine claims, determine eligibility, calculate taxes or offsets, price insurance or measure an illness probability. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Health insurance: critical illness cover ↗

    Official HTML reviewed 25 October 2026; page dated 16 October 2025. Supports the usual one-time payment structure and insurer-specific definitions. No listed condition is treated as an automatic approved claim.

  2. FCAC · Disability insurance ↗

    Official HTML reviewed 25 October 2026; page dated 31 July 2026. Supports checking definitions, amount, timing, duration, tax and offsets. The calculator assumes independently confirmed net amounts and calculates none of those contract or tax rules.
